claim.author: R0b-models builder
claim.card: A model is called better than predicting without its predictors only when its gain's interval lies above zero and the gain exceeds {min_gain} on a score where higher is better, or {min_gain:.0%} of the baseline's own loss on a loss such as log loss.
claim.methods: A family was called better than its no-predictor baseline only when the gain's corrected interval lay above zero and the gain exceeded a floor, a convention: {min_gain} on a score better when higher, and on a loss {min_gain:.0%} of the baseline's own cross-validated loss (a McFadden pseudo R squared, a ranked probability skill score or a scaled Brier score of {min_gain}).

min_gain.unit: on a score better when higher, its own scale; on a loss, a share of the baseline's loss

basis.reason: A convention, not a cited rule (baseline.py): no source sets one smallest gain that matters for every outcome.

R² is already the MSE's gain as a share of the baseline's, and a McFadden R², a ranked probability skill score and a scaled Brier score are the same share of log loss, the RPS and the Brier score at the horizon, so one share reads alike across them. A fixed 0.01 on a loss's own scale called a rare outcome's true risks, gaining 6% to 12% of the baseline's loss, better by too little to matter (claims backtest A-029; the silent test's construction).

regime.words: a family's cross-validated primary against its no-predictor baseline under Predict, paired over the same folds: R² for a numeric outcome, log loss for a yes/no or class outcome, the ranked probability score for an ordered one, the Brier score at the horizon for time to event

claim.author: R0b-models builder
claim.card: Below {small_rows} training rows the shelf rates boosted trees fair, and poor below {tiny_rows}: they overfit easily and their cross-validated score is noisy.
claim.methods: On the shelf, boosted trees (and XGBoost, read through them) were rated fair below {small_rows} training rows and poor below {tiny_rows}, a convention.

basis.reason: A convention carried from draft 2's shelf scores: RECIPES §2.6 says no validated rule predicts which family will perform best, and states boosted trees' rows nowhere.
Fewer rows let a boosted ensemble fit noise and make a cross-validated score noisier, a general expectation the shelf orders by, not a measured threshold.

regime.words: the shelf's pre-fit rating of boosted trees, and of XGBoost through it, read on the training rows under either purpose

claim.author: R0b-models builder
claim.card: Below {small_rows} training rows the shelf rates a random forest fair: its cross-validated score is noisy.
claim.methods: On the shelf, the random forest was rated fair below {small_rows} training rows, a convention.

basis.reason: RECIPES §2.6's table: 2.0 from 2,000 training rows, 1.5 from 500, fair at 1.0 below 500, a convention, since no validated rule predicts which family will perform best.
Fewer rows make a cross-validated score noisier, a general expectation the shelf orders by, not a measured threshold; the forest's rating has no poor step below it, as boosted trees' does.

regime.words: the shelf's pre-fit rating of the random forest, read on the training rows under either purpose

claim.author: R0b-models builder
claim.card: Under Predict, both of a nearly collinear pair are kept and their importance read together, a convention set for you to confirm: such a pair does not harm prediction on rows like these.
claim.methods: Under Predict, both predictors of a nearly collinear pair were kept and their importance read together, a convention the analyst confirmed rather than a decision: collinearity does not harm prediction on rows like the training rows, and the elastic-net selection filter, a step before every family, was offered but not recommended.

basis.reason: Collinearity inflates the variance of the pair's separate coefficients, not of predictions on rows like the training rows; the fires test's construction (a pair at r = 0.95, ten draws) shows the elastic-net filter keeps both, leaves least squares where it was and harms the forest. New rows where the pair comes apart are outside it.
BEATS_PREDICT M4 sets keeping the pair as a convention for the person to confirm; no materiality instrument grades it under Predict.

regime.words: Predict, a pair of numeric predictors nearly collinear on the training rows (explore's pair scan), scored on new rows like the training rows

claim.ruled: calm/BEATS_PREDICT.md M4, its fourth line (near-collinear predictors; grouped importance)

claim.author: R0b-models builder
claim.card: The share of rows an energy screen removes, times how far they differ on what the model adjusts for, is a screening convention: it can say the screen could bias the estimate or that you should act on it, never that it doesn't change your numbers here.
claim.methods: Rows changed times the leavers' largest standardized mean difference on the adjustment set served as an outcome-blind screening convention floored at could bias, not as a predictor of how far the estimate moves: what moves a correctly specified coefficient is what the leavers report of the exposure, not their imbalance on what is adjusted for.

basis.reason: Both backtest referees and the adjudicator found the product does not track the coefficient's movement (claims backtest A-124), and the fires test constructs a screen below the committed cut-off that moves the estimate by most of its half-width; its nine calibration cases come from one fixture.
The floor is the convention's own (its floored reason in materiality_calibration.json): a proxy without it may still be calibrated, and band 2 stays band 2.

regime.words: the energy screen's noticing (diet-implausible-reporters) under Estimate, before the lock: the predicted movement of keeping every row, read as rows changed times the leavers' largest SMD on the adjustment set, whatever its calibration cases

claim.author: R0b-models builder
claim.card: Below an effective size of {small_n}, boosted trees and XGBoost are not tuned: each is fit once at a small-sample standard, which in simulation predicted about as well as tuning and stayed calibrated, where the libraries' defaults did not.
claim.methods: Below an effective size of {small_n} (units for a numeric outcome; events, or the rarest class's count, for a yes/no or class outcome) the tuning plan drew no candidate settings for a searched family, and boosted trees and XGBoost were fit once at a small-sample standard chosen by simulation in place of the libraries' defaults; from {small_n} their settings were searched inside every training fold, the defaults among the candidates.

small_n.unit: units of effective size (units, events or the rarest class's count, in one outer training fold)

basis.reason: RECIPES §4.6 calls 300 a convention, and the 2026-10-11 ruling kept it: the small-sample study's cells all sat below it (at or above 300 in 1 of 680 datasets), so the study does not locate the threshold.

notes/SMALL_SAMPLE_STANDARD.md: across 14 small-sample cells the libraries' defaults were the worst arm in every one (regret 0.10 to 0.39 nats, calibration slopes 0.2 to 0.5), and the standard matched nested tuning to the K floor on loss with a third of its calibration spread. Its constants were chosen with every cell in view, so those cells are not held out; test_small_sample_standard.py checks it again on T1's signal generator at n = 200.

The study fit the two boosting families on ten normal predictors with a yes/no outcome, a numeric one checked; multiclass and ordered outcomes, categorical predictors, p = 50 and NHANES subsamples are not yet checked (RECIPES §4.6, before release), though the plan applies the standard to every task.

regime.words: boosted trees or XGBoost under Predict on a yes/no or numeric outcome, the plan's effective size below the threshold: the regime of notes/SMALL_SAMPLE_STANDARD.md's simulation (ten normal predictors, 100 to 1,000 rows, a yes/no outcome chosen on and a numeric one checked)
